title: Kinship care preserves family continuity while redistributing hidden household capacity
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office GAO-26-107658; nationally representative Census/HHS kinship-family characteristics and selected community/caregiver support evidence
geography: United States kinship families, with selected communities in Mississippi, New Mexico, and Oklahoma and caregiver interviews from 10 states and two Tribes

denominator.unit: children raised by relatives or close family friends because parents were unable to care for them

kinship_to_foster_ratio.unit: children in kinship families not in foster care per one child in foster care, approximate reported ratio

formal_route_boundary.value: families with children in foster care may access financial and other resources if caregivers meet state requirements, while other kinship families may be ineligible

observations.method: GAO analysis of nationally representative Census Bureau and HHS data for 2019–2023; 2020 Census data excluded because of collection differences.
observations.uncertainty: The population frame is not all multigenerational households or all informal caregiving; the 18-to-1 comparison is not a resource-need ratio, causal estimate, or evidence that non-foster families need the same intervention.
observations.subgroup: Children raised by relatives or close family friends because parents cannot care for them, separated by foster-care status where reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Kinship arrangements can preserve family, community, culture, school, and stability; formal foster status may change eligibility without determining the quality, safety, or sustainability of daily care.

observations.period: 2023; kinship-family household, caregiver, and child characteristics

denominator.unit: national kinship-family households and children; measure-specific denominators vary and are not disclosed in this record

poverty_context.value: kinship families were more likely than all families to live in poverty

caregiver_context.value: households were typically headed by grandparents, who were more likely than the general population to have a disability and be out of the labor force

child_need_context.value: children living with grandparents more often had physical or mental health issues and special-education needs

observations.method: GAO analysis of nationally representative Census/HHS data and review of kinship-family characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: These are descriptive associations; they do not establish whether kinship care caused poverty, caregiver labor-force exit, disability, child health or education needs, or the intensity and quality of care.
observations.subgroup: Kinship families, grandparent-headed households, children living with grandparents, and comparison families/populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Caregiver age, disability, labor-force status, household resources, and child needs may precede the arrangement, respond to it, or jointly shape it; family care can be protective and costly at the same time.

observations.period: 2023–2025; selected community and caregiver challenge/resource evidence

denominator.unit: communities reviewed across three counties and three Tribes in Mississippi, New Mexico, and Oklahoma; plus 16 caregiver interviews from 10 states and two Tribes

persistent_challenges.value: some kinship families continued to report unmet childcare and affordable-housing needs; some officials and most interviewed caregivers reported worsened cost-of-living or mental-health challenges since the pandemic

resource_variation.value: resources and supports varied across the six communities; foster-care-specific resources were discussed in all communities

federal_role.value: HHS leads awareness/collaboration efforts and administers funds through programs states may use to support kinship families

observations.method: GAO site visits, interviews with local officials and 16 kinship caregivers, and federal program/interagency document review.
observations.uncertainty: The selected communities and caregiver interviews are not representative; reported challenge, resource availability, referral, eligibility, receipt, caregiver burden, child outcome, and later stability are separate stages.
observations.subgroup: Selected counties, Tribes, local officials, service providers, and interviewed kinship caregivers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local variation may reflect different community assets, tribal or state structures, provider networks, or awareness; federal funding availability does not establish local capacity or successful support.

related_sources.claim: Official GAO review supplies kinship-family population scale, foster/non-foster distinction, household characteristics, selected challenges, resources, federal support, methods, and limits.

boundary: This record establishes a kinship-family, intergenerational care, formal-support, and selected community-resource surface. It does not establish caregiver hours, cost, employment change, housing move, child safety or school outcome, benefit receipt, respite, placement stability, reunification, caregiver exhaustion, trust, or exit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO HTML report page retrieved and hashed; report PDF, Census/HHS microdata, case records, community directories, and caregiver files not retained
